x.ASV: Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said,
x.Darby: And Bildad the Shuhite answered and said,
x.KJV: Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said,
x.YLT: And Bildad the Shuhite answereth and saith: --

x.ASV: How long wilt thou speak these things? And how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a mighty wind?
x.Darby: How long wilt thou speak these things? and the words of thy mouth be a strong wind?
x.KJV: How long wilt thou speak these things? and how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind?
x.YLT: Till when dost thou speak these things? And a strong wind--sayings of thy mouth?

nt: Bildad is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Until when will you say these things, and until when will the words of your mouth be a mighty wind]

Bildad is using the question form for emphasis. If you would not use the question form for that purpose in your language, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not keep saying these things, and the words of your mouth should not keep being a mighty wind!]

Bildad is using the term **mouth** to mean speaking, by association with the way people use their mouths to speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the words that you speak] or see next note for another possibility.
It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would be unnatural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [your words] or [what you say]

Bildad is speaking as if the **words** of Job were literally a **mighty wind**. He means that Job is saying many things insistently, but they are not substantial. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and … be so insistent but so insubstantial]

x.ASV: Doth God pervert justice? Or doth the Almighty pervert righteousness?
x.Darby: DothGod pervert judgment, and the Almighty pervert justice?
x.KJV: Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice?
x.YLT: Doth God pervert judgment? And doth the Mighty One pervert justice?

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **justice** and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Does God do things that are not just? Does the Almighty do things that are not righteous?]

Bildad is using the question form for emphasis. If you would not use the question form for that purpose in your language, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God does not pervert justice! No, the Almighty does not pervert righteousness!] or, positively, [God always does what is just! Yes, the Almighty always does what is righteous!]

x.ASV: If thy children have sinned against him, And he hath delivered them into the hand of their transgression;
x.Darby: If thy children have sinned against him, he hath also given them over into the hand of their transgression.
x.KJV: If thy children have sinned against him, and he have cast them away for their transgression;
x.YLT: If thy sons have sinned before Him, And He doth send them away, By the hand of their transgression,

nt: In this context, to be **in the hand of** someone or something means to be under the power or control of that person or thing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then he put them under the power of their sins] or [then he put them under the control of their sins]

Bildad is speaking as if the **sins** of Job’s **children** were a living thing that had exerted power over them and killed them. He actually means that God killed Job’s children in order to punish them for their sins. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then God punished them by killing them for the sins they committed]

x.ASV: If thou wouldest seek diligently unto God, And make thy supplication to the Almighty;
x.Darby: If thou seek earnestly untoGod, and make thy supplication to the Almighty,
x.KJV: If thou wouldest seek unto God betimes, and make thy supplication to the Almighty;
x.YLT: If thou dost seek early unto God, And unto the Mighty makest supplication,

nt: For emphasis, Bildad is stating the pronoun **you**, whose meaning is already present in the verb translated **seek diligently**. If your language can state implied pronouns explicitly for emphasis, you may want to use that construction here in your translation. Other languages may have other ways of bringing out this emphasis. Alternate translation: [If you seek diligently for God yourself]

Bildad is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and if to the Almighty you appeal]

x.ASV: If thou wert pure and upright: Surely now he would awake for thee, And make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous.
x.Darby: If thou be pure and upright, surely now he will awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous;
x.KJV: If thou wert pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous.
x.YLT: If pure and upright thou art, Surely now He waketh for thee, And hath completed The habitation of thy righteousness.

nt: The terms **pure** and **upright** mean similar things. Bildad is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [truly righteous]

One possible meaning of the expression translated **rouse himself** is “wake up.” If there is already a Bible translation in your region, it may say something like this. Bildad could be speaking as if God were sleeping and would literally wake up at the realization that Job needed and deserved help. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will come quickly to help you]

Bildad is using one aspect of Job, his **righteousness**, to mean all of him as a righteous person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your habitation as a righteous person]

Bildad is speaking of the situation that he believes Job would deserve as a righteous person as if that situation were literally a **habitation** or place where Job would live. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [restore you to the situation in life that a righteous person deserves]

x.ASV: And though thy beginning was small, Yet thy latter end would greatly increase.
x.Darby: And though thy beginning was small, yet thine end shall be very great.
x.KJV: Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase.
x.YLT: And thy beginning hath been small, And thy latter end is very great.

nt: וְ⁠הָיָ֣ה רֵאשִׁיתְ⁠ךָ֣ מִצְעָ֑ר וְ֝⁠אַחֲרִיתְ⁠ךָ֗ יִשְׂגֶּ֥ה מְאֹֽד

Since, as [1:3](../01/03.md) states, Job was previously the greatest man in a vast area, it is not the case that his **beginning**, that is, his former condition, was **small**. Bildad actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying. He means that Job’s former state, great though it was, will seem small by comparison with the much greater prosperity that Job will experience in the future if he seeks God diligently. Alternate translation: [Though your former state was great, your future will be so much greater that the former state will seem as if it had been small]

Bildad is speaking of Job’s **end**, that is, his ultimate condition in life, as if it were a living thing that could **increase**. He means that Job’s prosperity will increase greatly in the end. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [yet your prosperity will increase greatly in the end]

x.ASV: For inquire, I pray thee, of the former age, And apply thyself to that which their fathers have searched out
x.Darby: For inquire, I pray thee, of the former generation, and attend to the researches of their fathers;
x.KJV: For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers:
x.YLT: For, ask I pray thee of a former generation, And prepare to a search of their fathers,

nt: Bildad is speaking as if Job could literally ask the people of **former generations** for advice. He means that Job should consider the wisdom that those people passed down to their descendants through tradition. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [consider the traditional wisdom that the former generations have passed down to us]
Bildad is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If your readers would misunderstand this, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their ancestors]

x.ASV: (For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, Because our days upon earth are a shadow);
x.Darby: For we are [but] of yesterday, and know nothing, for our days upon earth are a shadow.
x.KJV: (For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow:)
x.YLT: (For of yesterday we are, and we know not, For a shadow are our days on earth.)

nt: Bildad is saying that he, Job, and the other two friends were only born **yesterday** and that they do **not know** anything. He says both of these things as overstatements for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [we have not been alive for very long and we do not know very much]

By **we** and **our**, Bildad means himself and the other friends and also Job, to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of those words in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Bildad is speaking as if the **days** that he and Job and the other friends have **on earth** were literally a **shadow**. He means that just as a shadow appears only for a short time, so people are only on earth for a short time. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our days on earth are fleeting]
Bildad is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our time on earth is a shadow]

x.ASV: Shall not they teach thee, and tell thee, And utter words out of their heart?
x.Darby: Shall not they teach thee, [and] tell thee, and utter words out of their heart?
x.KJV: Shall not they teach thee, and tell thee, and utter words out of their heart?
x.YLT: Do they not shew thee--speak to thee, And from their heart bring forth words?

nt: הֲ⁠לֹא־הֵ֣ם י֭וֹרוּ⁠ךָ יֹ֣אמְרוּ לָ֑⁠ךְ וּ֝⁠מִ⁠לִּבָּ֗⁠ם יוֹצִ֥אוּ מִלִּֽים

The pronouns **they** and **their** refer to the “former generations,” that is, the ancestors whom Bildad described in [verse 8](../08/08.md). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Will the former generations not teach you? Our ancestors will speak to you, and from their hearts they will bring forth words]
הֲ⁠לֹא־הֵ֣ם י֭וֹרוּ⁠ךָ יֹ֣אמְרוּ לָ֑⁠ךְ וּ֝⁠מִ⁠לִּבָּ֗⁠ם יוֹצִ֥אוּ מִלִּֽים

Bildad is speaking as if Job’s ancestors would **teach** him and **speak to** him. He does not mean this literally. Instead, he means that Job can learn from the accumulated wisdom that has been passed down to them from their ancestors through tradition. Bildad will summarize this traditional teaching in the rest of his speech. Particularly if there is a practice of ancestor worship in your culture, be sure to make this meaning clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [You can learn much from the traditional teachings we have received from them. It would be as if they were speaking to you and bringing forth words from their hearts]

Bildad is using the question form for emphasis. If you would not use the question form for that purpose in your language, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [They will certainly teach you.]

Bildad is speaking as if the ancestors would literally **bring forth words** from **their hearts**, as if their hearts were containers that held words and as if words were physical objects that someone could **bring forth**. He is using the word **hearts** to mean a person’s thoughts and emotions. He is saying that through tradition the ancestors have passed down their most cherished beliefs and the most profound lessons they learned in life. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will share with you their most cherished insights]

x.ASV: Can the rush grow up without mire? Can the flag grow without water?
x.Darby: Doth the papyrus shoot up without mire? doth the reed-grass grow without water?
x.KJV: Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?
x.YLT: `Doth a rush wise without mire? A reed increase without water?

nt: From here to the end of the chapter, Bildad may be quoting the teaching of the ancestors. This would be a second-level quotation, since the book is already quoting Bildad’s speech. If you think it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate the start of this possible quotation from tradition with an opening second-level quotation mark or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate the start of a second-level quotation.

Bildad is using the question form for emphasis. If you would not use the question form for that purpose in your language, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [Papyrus does not grow without a marsh. A reed does not grow without waters.]

The word **papyrus** describes a tall, reed-like plant that grows in shallow water. If your readers would not be familiar with what papyrus is, in your translation you could use the name of a comparable plant in your area, or you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [a bulrush] or [a cattail]

x.ASV: Whilst it is yet in its greenness, and not cut down, It withereth before any other herb.
x.Darby: Whilst it is yet in its greenness [and] not cut down, it withereth before any [other] grass.
x.KJV: Whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb.
x.YLT: While it is in its budding--uncropped, Even before any herb it withereth.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **greenness**, you could express the same idea in another way. The idea is that while marsh plants dry up and lose color at the end of their life cycles, this is a young plant that is still colorful and growing. Alternate translation: [young and growing]

Bildad assumes that Job will understand that he means that even a young, uncut reed **withers** without water. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [but without water it withers before any other plant]

Bildad says **any** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [but without water it withers very quickly]

x.ASV: So are the paths of all that forget God; And the hope of the godless man shall perish:
x.Darby: So are the paths of all that forgetGod; and the profane man's hope shall perish,
x.KJV: So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite’s hope shall perish:
x.YLT: So are the paths of all forgetting God, And the hope of the profane doth perish,

nt: Bildad is speaking of the things that happen to people as if they were literally **paths** that those people were walking along. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This is what happens to all the ones forgetting God]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hope**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the godless will not get what they hope for]

Bildad is using the adjective **godless** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this word with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a godless person]

x.ASV: Whose confidence shall break in sunder, And whose trust is a spider’s web.
x.Darby: Whose confidence shall be cut off, and his reliance is a spider's web.
x.KJV: Whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider’s web.
x.YLT: Whose confidence is loathsome, And the house of a spider his trust.

nt: Bildad is speaking as if the **confidence** of a person who is godless literally **snaps** and as if the **trust** of a godless person were literally a spider’s web (**the house of a spider**). If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whose confidence proves unfounded and whose trust is unreliable]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **confidence** and **trust**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. It may be helpful to begin a new sentence here. Alternate translation: [He is confident that certain things will happen, but they do not happen; he trusts in certain people and things to help him, but they do not]

Bildad is using **the house of a spider** (that is, a spider’s web) to represent something flimsy and unreliable. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and whose trust is as flimsy and unreliable as a spider’s web]

x.ASV: He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand: He shall hold fast thereby, but it shall not endure.
x.Darby: He shall lean upon his house, and it shall not stand; he shall lay hold on it, but it shall not endure.
x.KJV: He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand: he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure.
x.YLT: He leaneth on his house--and it standeth not: He taketh hold on it--and it abideth not.

nt: יִשָּׁעֵ֣ן עַל־בֵּ֭ית⁠וֹ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יַעֲמֹ֑ד יַחֲזִ֥יק בּ֝֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יָקֽוּם

Bildad is speaking of a godless person as if he were literally leaning against his **house** and causing it to collapse beyond repair. The house represents the possessions and status of the godless person. Alternate translation: [It does not take much for a godless person to lose his possessions and status without any hope of recovering them]
If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use positive statements in your translation in place of these negative ones. Alternate translation: [and it collapses … but it remains collapsed]

Bildad is speaking of the **house** of a godless person as if it were a living thing that could **arise** on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but he cannot make it stand upright again] or [but he cannot repair it]

x.ASV: He is green before the sun, And his shoots go forth over his garden.
x.Darby: He is full of sap before the sun, and his sprout shooteth forth over his garden;
x.KJV: He is green before the sun, and his branch shooteth forth in his garden.
x.YLT: Green he is before the sun, And over his garden his branch goeth out.

nt: רָטֹ֣ב ה֭וּא לִ⁠פְנֵי־שָׁ֑מֶשׁ וְ⁠עַ֥ל גַּ֝נָּת֗⁠וֹ יֹֽנַקְתּ֥⁠וֹ תֵצֵֽא

Bildad now speaks of a godless person as if he were a plant. In order to depict the temporary prosperity that godless people may enjoy, he describes this plant flourishing. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning as a comparison. Alternate translation: [A godless person may at first thrive like a plant that is getting plenty of sunlight and whose shoots extend all over the garden in which it is planted]

Here the word **to the face of** means “in front of” or “in the presence of” something. Bildad means that the plant is **lush** because it receives plenty of sunlight. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because it receives plenty of sunlight]

x.ASV: His roots are wrapped about the stone -heap, He beholdeth the place of stones.
x.Darby: His roots are entwined about the stoneheap; he seeth the place of stones.
x.KJV: His roots are wrapped about the heap, and seeth the place of stones.
x.YLT: By a heap his roots are wrapped, A house of stones he looketh for.

nt: עַל־גַּ֭ל שָֽׁרָשָׁ֣י⁠ו יְסֻבָּ֑כוּ בֵּ֖ית אֲבָנִ֣ים יֶחֱזֶֽה

Bildad is continuing to speak of the godless person and his temporary prosperity as if he were a plant. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A godless person may at first be secure, like a plant whose roots are wrapped around a heap of stones, a plant that is solidly rooted among stones]

If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [It wraps its roots around a heap of stones]

Bildad is speaking as if this plant were looking for a **house** to live in. He means that the plant naturally roots itself in a secure place among **rocks**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it roots itself in a secure place among rocks]

x.ASV: If he be destroyed from his place, Then it shall deny him, saying, I have not seen thee.
x.Darby: If he destroy him from his place, then it shall deny him: I have not seen thee!
x.KJV: If he destroy him from his place, then it shall deny him, saying, I have not seen thee.
x.YLT: If one doth destroy him from his place, Then it hath feigned concerning him, I have not seen thee!

nt: In this verse, Bildad is drawing a contrast between the prosperity he described in the previous two verses and the inevitable destruction of the godless person. In your translation, you may wish to introduce this verse in a way that will indicate this contrast more explicitly. Alternate translation: [But when]

The pronoun **it** refers in its first and third instances to the plant Bildad has been describing, and it refers in its second instance to the **place** the plant was occupying. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [When one destroys such a plant from its place, then the place it formerly occupied will deny it]
It may be more natural in your language to have an indirect quotation here. Alternate translation: [It will deny that it ever saw it]

Bildad is speaking of the plant’s location as if it were a living thing that could recognize things and speak. The meaning of this phrase is similar to the meaning of the phrase “his place will not know him again” in [7:10](../07/10.md). In this case, Bildad is saying that the plant will be so thoroughly removed that its former location will be convinced that it was never there to begin with. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it will be as if it had never been there at all]

x.ASV: Behold, this is the joy of his way; And out of the earth shall others spring.
x.Darby: Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the dust shall others grow.
x.KJV: Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the earth shall others grow.
x.YLT: Lo, this is the joy of his way, And from the dust others spring up.'

nt: Bildad actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of his words. He is speaking in this way for emphasis. He does not mean that the godless person has actual **joy**. Such a person may have temporary prosperity, but he then experiences sorrow as a consequence of the way he has been living. Alternate translation: [the sorrow of his way]

Bildad is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the sorrow that comes from his conduct]

Bildad is continuing to speak as if the godless person were a plant. When he says that **other plants** will **sprout** from the **dust** (that is, the ground), he means that other people will take the place of the godless person when his conduct causes his ruin. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and other people will take his position and his possessions]

x.ASV: Behold, God will not cast away a perfect man, Neither will he uphold the evil-doers.
x.Darby: Behold,God will not cast off a perfect man, neither will he take evil-doers by the hand.
x.KJV: Behold, God will not cast away a perfect man, neither will he help the evil doers:
x.YLT: Lo, God doth not reject the perfect, Nor taketh hold on the hand of evil doers.

nt: If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this double negative that consists of the negative particle **not** and the negative verb **reject**. Alternate translation: [God will always accept the innocent]

Bildad is using the adjective **innocent** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this word with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a person who is innocent]

Bildad is speaking as if God would literally **hold** evildoers by the **hand** in order to keep them from falling down. He means that God does not strengthen or support people who do evil. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but he will not help evildoers]

x.ASV: He will yet fill thy mouth with laughter, And thy lips with shouting.
x.Darby: Whilst he would fill thy mouth with laughing and thy lips with shouting,
x.KJV: Till he fill thy mouth with laughing, and thy lips with rejoicing.
x.YLT: While he filleth with laughter thy mouth, And thy lips with shouting,

nt: Bildad is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and he will fill your lips with shouting]

Bildad is speaking of Job’s **mouth** as if it were a container that God would **fill** with **laughter** and as if Job’s **lips** were a container that God would fill with **shouting**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will yet make you shout very joyfully]

Bildad is using parts of Job, his **mouth** and his **lips**, to mean all of Job in the acts of laughing and shouting joyfully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will yet make you laugh very happily and shout very joyfully]

x.ASV: They that hate thee shall be clothed with shame; And the tent of the wicked shall be no more.
x.Darby: They that hate thee shall be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked be no more.
x.KJV: They that hate thee shall be clothed with shame; and the dwelling place of the wicked shall come to nought.
x.YLT: Those hating thee do put on shame, And the tent of the wicked is not!

nt: Bildad is speaking as if Job’s enemies would literally **wear shame** as if it were their clothing. He means that they will be greatly ashamed for opposing Job when God honors and restores him. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will be greatly ashamed]

Bildad is using one possession of **the wicked**, the **tent** in which they live, to mean all of their possessions and their standing in the community. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the wicked will be without status or means]

Bildad is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this word with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

If you decided to punctuate [verses 11–22](../08/11.md) as a second-level quotation, indicate the end of this quotation here with a closing second-level quotation mark or whatever other punctuation or convention your language uses to indicate the end of a second-level quotation.
